items: Shape A has at most one recursive child per frame. Across n linked nodes, it creates one chain with O(n) calls and O(n) maximum depth.

Shape B has two recursive children for most positive n. Without memoization, states such as fib(n - 2) are reached through multiple branches, so the call tree has exponential total work even though its depth is O(n).

blocks.text: Both functions are recursive and both progress toward a base, so those facts alone do not determine cost. The transfer rule is to classify branching factor, subproblem sizes, and overlap before assigning a complexity class. Exact stack accounting is owned by the stack-and-complexity unit.

Smaller arguments prove progress, not linear work. B revisits many sizes through two branches, so the total number of calls grows much faster than its depth.

blocks.text:
Both an outline section and an expression node own recursively nested children. The local node contributes a
rule—add its own words in the outline, or apply its operator in the expression—while each child is delegated
to the same function contract. Repeated symbols, parentheses, or a known depth can be useful context, but
none is sufficient evidence of self-similarity. This transfer boundary also separates recursive syntax from
recursive structure: a flat token stream may be processed iteratively until it is parsed into nested
expressions. The item trains recognition of the structural contract, not a choice between preorder and
postorder traversal.

messages.text: A known bound can help allocate resources, but it does not define how the current result reduces to results of smaller expressions. The recursive contract comes from the child-expression structure.
Repeated vocabulary is only a surface cue. Recursion is justified by operands being complete nested expressions, not by seeing the same operator token more than once.

Parentheses can occur in a flat or already parsed representation and do not by themselves establish a smaller same-contract object. The structural relationship between an expression and its operand expressions is decisive.

feedback.reason: An operand is not merely related data; it is a smaller complete instance of the evaluation problem.

blocks.text:
The decisive signal is recursive containment: a section contains child sections, and each child can be
solved by the same function that solves the parent. The parent contributes its own word count exactly once
and delegates each smaller subtree to the same contract. A self-call on the unchanged section is only
recursive syntax; it is not a smaller subproblem. Flattening may still produce a correct iterative solution,
but it is a different decomposition and does not explain the natural recursion. This transfer works for
acyclic nested ownership such as folders, comments, and expression nodes. A general graph needs an
additional visited-state contract because a child reference may lead back to an already seen node.

messages.text: Flattening can be a valid separate preprocessing strategy, but it avoids rather than identifies the direct self-similar subproblem. The recursive observation is that every child is itself a complete section subtree with the same total contract.
The self-call may look recursive, but it does not move to a smaller structure. The same section is requested again, so no recursive decomposition has been established.
Depth describes position, not the contents of the subtree. Two sections at the same depth can contain different words and descendants, so depth alone cannot represent the required subproblem.

feedback.reason: Each direct subsection is a smaller object governed by the same total-word-count contract.

blocks.text:
Recursion stops when the current problem has become atomic under the chosen decomposition. A crossed
interval has no characters, and a single-position interval has one character but no pair to compare. Both
are already palindromes under this contract. A two-character interval is different: its one outer pair is
still the material decision. This boundary shows why recursive structure is not tied to an empty-input
keyword. The terminal shape follows from what the recursive step removes. The same reasoning applies when
peeling matching delimiters, trimming equal endpoints, or consuming two items per call: both zero-item and
one-item remainders may be atomic.

messages.text: Intervals with at least two positions still contain an outer pair whose equality determines whether recursion may continue. Treating all non-empty states as terminal skips the actual decision.
A two-character interval still has one material pair to compare. It may recurse to the crossed state after that comparison, but it is not yet pair-free.
The crossed interval is the zero-character terminal shape produced after removing the last pair.
A single character is already palindromic and contains no two-ended pair to decompose.

feedback.reason: Crossed and single-position intervals have no remaining pair, even though only one of them is empty.

blocks.text:
The function contract is uniform: countDown(n) means the number of one-step decrements from n to zero.
Calls with 4, 3, 2, 1, and 0 therefore have different state values but identical semantic form. This
distinction is essential. If identical values were required, no progress could occur; if the contract
changed at each value, the parent could not interpret the child's return. The same principle transfers to
suffix indices, remaining lengths, tree children, and interval bounds: the state varies while the contract
remains stable.

messages.text: The arguments change, but every frame still promises the same meaning: the number of decrements from its own n to 0. Changing the contract per frame would make returned values impossible to compose reliably.
Recursion repeats a function contract, not an identical state value. Keeping n unchanged would prevent the subproblem from becoming smaller.
A self-reference identifies recursive syntax, but a usable recursive decomposition also requires the nested call to represent a legitimate smaller instance of the same problem.
